title: Long-term weight loss effects of semaglutide in obesity without diabetes in the SELECT trial
question: In adults with cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity but no diabetes, how much weight did weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg take off over 4 years compared with placebo, and was it safe across body sizes?

bottom_line.question: In adults with cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity but no diabetes, how much weight did weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg take off over 4 years compared with placebo, and was it safe across body sizes?
bottom_line.answer: By week 208, mean body weight had changed by −10.2% with semaglutide and −1.5% with placebo, a treatment difference of −8.7%; weight fell until week 65 and then held.

provenance.quote: For those in the semaglutide group, the weight-loss trajectory continued to week 65 and then was sustained for the study period through week 208 (−10.2% for the semaglutide group, −1.5% for the placebo group; treatment difference −8.7%; 95% CI −9.42 to −7.88; P < 0.0001).

sections.title: Why the Study Was Done
sections.markdown:
Worldwide obesity, defined as a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or more, has nearly tripled since 1975. Excess body fat drives cardiovascular disease and adds to diabetes, kidney disease and cancer. The most harmful kinds are **visceral fat**, which is packed around the organs, and ectopic fat, which is stored in places it doesn't belong. Health measures such as heart risk factors, blood sugar and quality of life start to improve after about 5% weight loss, and larger losses help more. Diet and exercise alone rarely produce weight loss that is both large and lasting.

Drugs that change appetite make a loss of 10% or more more likely. Semaglutide belongs to a class of these drugs called GLP-1 receptor agonists. As a once-weekly 2.4 mg injection under the skin, it is approved for long-term weight management. Lower doses are approved for type 2 diabetes.

The SELECT trial tested whether semaglutide 2.4 mg prevents heart attacks, strokes and cardiovascular deaths in people who already had heart disease and were overweight or obese but did not have diabetes. It cut these events by 20% (hazard ratio 0.80, 95% confidence interval 0.72 to 0.90). The analysis summarized here was planned before the data came in. It asks different questions of the same trial:

- how much weight people lost, and whether they kept it off for four years
- how waist size changed
- whether safety depended on starting body size

Because SELECT ran for up to 208 weeks, it is the longest placebo-controlled trial of semaglutide's effect on weight.

sections.title: How the Trial Was Run and What Was Measured
sections.markdown:
## The trial

SELECT enrolled 17,604 adults from 41 countries between 2018 and 2021. Everyone was at least 45, had a BMI of 27 or more, and had established cardiovascular disease: a previous heart attack, a previous stroke, or symptomatic peripheral artery disease. The average participant was 61.6 years old with a BMI of 33.3, and 72.3% were men.

Participants were randomly split 1:1 between weekly semaglutide and placebo, and the trial was double-blind (neither patients nor doctors knew who got which). The semaglutide dose started at 0.24 mg and rose every four weeks until it reached 2.4 mg at week 16. If side effects were a problem, doctors could slow the increases, pause treatment, or keep a patient on a lower dose. Both groups got standard heart-disease care, which included lifestyle counseling that was not aimed at weight loss.

The team sorted participants into four BMI groups: overweight (under 30), class I obesity (30 to under 35), class II (35 to under 40) and class III (40 or more). These groups differed in makeup. Asian participants were 14.5% of the overweight group but only 2.2% of class III. Women were 20.8% of the overweight group and 45.5% of class III.

## What was measured

Besides weight, the researchers tracked **anthropometric measures**, simple body measurements that stand in for how much fat a person carries and where it sits. BMI is the best known:

BMI = weight in kilograms / (height in meters x height in meters)

BMI tracks body fat well across a population, but for one person it can mislead because it ignores where the fat is. So the team also measured waist circumference (halfway between the lowest rib and the top of the hip bone) and the waist-to-height ratio:

waist-to-height ratio = waist circumference / height

A ratio above 0.5 is the usual sign of raised cardiometabolic risk, meaning risk of heart and metabolic disease. The team also counted how many people fell below waist cutoffs that depend on sex and race: 80 cm for Asian women, 88 cm for non-Asian women and Asian men, and 102 cm for non-Asian men.

There are two ways of counting in the results. The main **in-trial** analysis follows the intention-to-treat principle: everyone who was randomized counts in their assigned group, whether or not they kept taking the drug. The "first on-treatment" analysis counts each person only until the first time they went more than 35 days without the drug. That shows what the drug does for people who stay on it. Most results are reported as a treatment difference:

treatment difference = change with semaglutide - change with placebo

Missing measurements were filled in statistically. The confidence intervals were not adjusted for the many comparisons made, so the authors warn against treating any single one as definitive.

sections.title: Weight Loss, Waist Size and Who Benefited Most
sections.markdown:
## Weight and waist results

People on semaglutide kept losing weight until about week 65 (roughly 15 months) and then held steady through week 208. At four years, the semaglutide group had lost an average of 10.2% of body weight, compared with 1.5% on placebo:

treatment difference = -10.2% - (-1.5%) = -8.7 percentage points (95% CI -9.42 to -7.88)

People who stayed on the drug (the first on-treatment analysis) lost 11.7%, compared with 1.5% on placebo, a difference of 10.2 points. The gap between the two analyses comes from people who stopped taking semaglutide.

At two years, these were the shares of each group reaching each weight-loss milestone:

- 5% or more: 67.8% on semaglutide vs 21.3% on placebo
- 10% or more: 44.2% vs 6.9%
- 15% or more: 22.9% vs 1.7%
- 20% or more: 11.0% vs 0.6%
- 25% or more: 4.9% vs 0.1%

Plots of each person's weight change show wide variation between individuals in both groups, with the semaglutide group shifted toward larger losses.

Waist size followed the same pattern as weight. At four years, waists had shrunk by 7.7 cm on semaglutide and 1.3 cm on placebo, a difference of 6.4 cm. The waist-cutoff analysis covered only people starting with a BMI under 35, because above that level waist measurement is harder and less accurate. In this group, about 15% of each arm started below their sex- and race-specific cutoff. At two years, 41.2% of the semaglutide group was below it, compared with 18.0% on placebo.

The average waist-to-height ratio at the start was 0.66. Even the lowest third of participants averaged above 0.62, well past the 0.5 threshold, so this population had large waists. At four years, the ratio had fallen by 6.9% on semaglutide and 1.0% on placebo.

BMI categories shifted as well. At two years, 52.4% of semaglutide patients had dropped at least one BMI category, compared with 15.7% on placebo. On semaglutide, 12.0% reached a healthy BMI under 25, compared with 1.2% on placebo. No one started in that range, because the entry criteria required a BMI of 27 or more. The share with obesity fell from 71.0% to 43.3% on semaglutide and from 71.9% to 67.9% on placebo.

## Who lost more and who lost less

A forest plot of prespecified subgroups showed clinically meaningful weight loss in every group, but the amount varied:

- Relative to placebo, women lost more than men (11.1 vs 7.5 percentage points).
- Younger participants lost slightly more than older ones.
- People with a lower starting BMI lost slightly less.
- Asian participants lost somewhat less (7.3 points more than placebo). The authors note that they were concentrated in the lowest BMI group, which lost less overall.

The age and BMI differences were statistically significant but small. Three factors made no difference: ethnicity (Hispanic or not), blood sugar status (prediabetes or normal) and kidney function. Every one of those subgroups showed a treatment difference of about 8.5 points.

sections.title: Safety and Tolerability
sections.markdown:
In SELECT's main results, 16.6% of semaglutide patients stopped the drug because of an adverse event, twice the 8.2% on placebo. Broken down by body size, the pattern was graded: the lower the starting BMI, the more often people stopped semaglutide. Placebo showed no such trend. The authors think people with smaller bodies may get a higher effective dose of the drug. They also say differences in motivation or in cultural attitudes toward body size could play a part.

Serious adverse events were less common on semaglutide overall (33.4% of patients vs 36.4% on placebo), mainly because there were fewer cardiovascular events and infections. This held in every BMI group. The rates below are events per 100 years of observation, which allows a fair comparison when people were followed for different lengths of time:

| BMI group | Semaglutide | Placebo |
|---|---|---|
| under 30 | 43.23 | 50.48 |
| 30 to under 35 | 43.54 | 49.66 |
| 35 to under 40 | 51.07 | 52.73 |
| 40 or more | 47.06 | 60.85 |

There was no evidence that the effect differed between BMI groups. Serious gut, liver or gallbladder events were no more common on semaglutide in any group, and no new safety signals appeared.

sections.title: What the Results Mean, Limitations and Bottom Line
sections.markdown:
## Why the weight loss was smaller than in an earlier trial

The earlier STEP 1 trial of the same dose found 14.9% weight loss at 68 weeks, compared with 2.4% on placebo. That is a 12.5-point difference, against 8.7 points in SELECT. The authors argue the smaller figure is expected, for three reasons:

- **Trial purpose.** SELECT was a heart-outcomes trial in which weight was a secondary measure. STEP 1 volunteers joined to lose weight and followed a structured program: eating 500 fewer calories a day and exercising 150 minutes a week.
- **Population.** STEP 1 enrolled younger, healthier people, many more women (73.1% vs 27.7% of the semaglutide groups), and people with a higher average BMI (37.8 vs 33.3).
- **Dosing.** SELECT's dosing was more flexible. By week 104, about 77% of SELECT patients still taking the drug were on the full 2.4 mg, compared with 89.6% in STEP 1 at week 68.

The larger loss in SELECT's on-treatment analysis fits this explanation.

## Why people with lower BMI lost less

People with a BMI under 30 lost a smaller share of their weight than people with obesity, even though they got the same drug and possibly a higher effective dose. Above a BMI of 30, losses were similar across the obesity classes. Look AHEAD, a trial of diet and exercise, saw the same pattern.

The authors offer an explanation based on the **settling point**, also called the set point. Every weight-loss treatment eventually levels off at a weight that matches a person's genes and environment, and people with a lower BMI may already be close to that point. The authors add that the health gains come from losing visceral and ectopic fat, not fat stored on the hips and thighs. If so, people with heart disease and a lower BMI may need to lose less total weight to benefit. They present this as a hypothesis for future studies to test.

## Limitations

- **Not a prevention trial.** Everyone in SELECT already had heart disease, so its heart results should not be applied to everyone with excess weight.
- **Small subgroups.** Some racial subgroups were too small to show differences.
- **BMI floor of 27.** The trial left out people with a BMI under 27. That excludes many Asian patients who qualify for obesity drugs at lower BMI and waist thresholds under their own countries' guidelines. The authors call for trials in this group.
- **No body composition data.** The trial did not measure fat mass, lean mass or muscle, so it cannot say what kind of tissue was lost.

## Bottom line

For four years, weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg was tested in a large, diverse group of adults with heart disease and excess weight but no diabetes. It produced 8.7 percentage points more weight loss than placebo, along with matching drops in waist size and waist-to-height ratio. Weight loss peaked at around 15 months and was maintained. Clinically meaningful loss occurred in both sexes and in every race, region and body-size group. Serious adverse events were less frequent than on placebo in every BMI group, although people with a lower BMI stopped the drug more often. The authors see these results as support for broad use of semaglutide 2.4 mg to reduce cardiovascular events in people with overweight or obesity and existing heart disease.

terms.definition: The mean change in the semaglutide group minus the mean change in the placebo group, adjusted for the baseline value. A negative figure means more weight lost with semaglutide.

The authors argue the smaller figure is expected, for three reasons:
Trial purpose.** SELECT was a heart-outcomes trial in which weight was a secondary measure.

Every weight-loss treatment eventually levels off at a weight that matches a person's genes and environment, and people with a lower BMI may already be close to that point.
anchors.quote: Perhaps persons with BMI <30 kg m−2 are closer to their settling point and have less weight to lose to reach it.

sources.Sec12/p2: We reported in the primary SELECT analysis that serious adverse events (SAEs) were reported by 2,941 patients (33.4%) in the semaglutide arm and by 3,204 patients (36.4%) in the placebo arm (P < 0.001). For this study, we analyzed SAE rates by person-years of treatment exposure for BMI classes (<30 kg m−2, 30 to <35 kg m−2, 35 to <40 kg m−2, and ≥40 kg m−2) and provide these data in . We also provide an analysis of the most common categories of SAEs. Semaglutide was associated with lower SAEs, primarily driven by CV event and infections. Within each obesity class (<30 kg m−2, 30 to <35 kg m−2, 35 to <40 kg m−2, and ≥40 kg m−2), there were fewer SAEs in the group receiving semaglutide compared with placebo. Rates (events per 100 years of observation) of SAEs were 43.23, 43.54, 51.07 and 47.06 for semaglutide and 50.48, 49.66, 52.73 and 60.85 for placebo, with no evidence of heterogeneity. There was no detectable difference in hepatobiliary or gastrointestinal SAEs comparing semaglutide with placebo in any of the four BMI classes we evaluated.
sources.Sec20/p1: The statistical analyses for the in-trial period were based on the intention-to-treat principle and included all randomized patients irrespective of adherence to semaglutide or placebo or changes to background medications. Continuous endpoints were analyzed using an analysis of covariance model with treatment as a fixed factor and baseline value of the endpoint as a covariate. Missing data at the landmark visit, for example, week 104, were imputed using a multiple imputation model and done separately for each treatment arm and included baseline value as a covariate and fit to patients having an observed data point (irrespective of adherence to randomized treatment) at week 104. The fit model is used to impute values for all patients with missing data at week 104 to create 500 complete data sets. Rubin’s rules were used to combine the results. Estimated means are provided with s.e.m., and estimated treatment differences are provided with 95% CI. Binary endpoints were analyzed using logistic regression with treatment and baseline value as a covariate, where missing data were imputed by first using multiple imputation as described above and then categorizing the imputed data according to the endpoint, for example, body weight percentage change at week 104 of <0%. Subgroup analyses for continuous and binary endpoints also included the subgroup and interaction between treatment and subgroup as fixed factors. Because some patients in both arms continued to be followed but were off treatment, we also analyzed weight loss by first on-treatment group (observation period until first time being off treatment for >35 days) to assess a more realistic picture of weight loss in those adhering to treatment. CIs were not adjusted for multiplicity and should therefore not be used to infer definitive treatment effects. All statistical analyses were performed with SAS software, version 9.4 TS1M5 (SAS Institute).
sources.Sec19/p1: The following endpoints relevant to this paper were assessed at randomization (week 0) to years 2, 3 and 4: change in body weight (%); proportion achieving weight loss ≥5%, ≥10%, ≥15% and ≥20%; change in WC (cm); and percentage change in WHtR (cm cm−1). Improvement in BMI category (defined as being in a lower BMI class) was assessed at week 104 compared with baseline according to BMI classes: healthy (BMI <25 kg m−2), overweight (25 to <30 kg m−2), class I obesity (30 to <35 kg m−2), class II obesity (35 to <40 kg m−2) and class III obesity (≥40 kg m−2). The proportions of individuals with BMI <35 or ≥35 kg m−2 who achieved sex- and race-specific cutoff points for WC (indicating increased metabolic risk) were evaluated at week 104. The WC cutoff points were as follows: Asian women <80 cm, non-Asian women <88 cm, Asian men <88 cm and non-Asian men <102 cm.
